title: From Caterpillar to Clinician: Becoming the Dentist I Prepared to Be
html:
Building the Cocoon

SHOFU ARTICLE PROGRAM

Written by: Branden Franzen

For years, I had been preparing for one particular moment: the day I would finally become a dentist.

Three years of undergraduate education, a year working in a dental laboratory, and four years of dental school had led me here. Along the way, I listened to hundreds of hours of podcasts about clinical dentistry, leadership, and practice ownership. I completed more than 300 hours of continuing education as a dental student, attended conventions, and had countless conversations with dentists, attorneys, CPAs, financial planners, bankers, coaches, marketers, and other professionals. I thought I was prepared. Then, I graduated.

I quickly realized that becoming a dentist isn’t a switch that gets flipped on graduation day. It is more like a butterfly emerging from its cocoon. The foundation has been built, but the world suddenly looks very different. Everything I had learned was still there, but now I was responsible for deciding how to use it. And, surprisingly, that uncertainty has been one of the most exciting parts of the journey.

Emerging From the Cocoon

One of the strangest parts of becoming a new dentist is realizing how many decisions you can finally make for yourself. During dental school, there was always another level of approval. Could I use this material? Was this treatment plan appropriate? Was this procedure within my experience level? Should I approach the case this way or that way? Those questions were necessary. They protected patients and helped me develop sound clinical judgment. But there was always an underlying understanding that I was still a student.

Now, that has changed. No longer do I have to ask a preceptor for permission to use a particular material. No longer am I told that a treatment plan is too complex because I am “just a dental student.” If I determine that a particular treatment is appropriate for my patient, I am now responsible for presenting that option and explaining it.

That freedom is exhilarating. It is also a tremendous responsibility. For the first time, my patients are not being treated according to what I am allowed to do as a student. They are being treated according to what I believe is clinically appropriate for them. That distinction has fundamentally changed the way I think about dentistry.

Learning to Spread My Wings

Graduation did not mean I stopped learning; if anything, it accelerated it. I walked into a practice with systems that were different from the ones I had spent years learning. The implant system was different. The endodontic system was different. The materials were different. The workflows were different. At the same time, I continued pursuing the areas of dentistry that excite me most. I have taken courses in complex soft-tissue grafting and full-arch implant therapy, and within my first month after graduation, I pursued IV moderate sedation certification because I want to provide patients with a more comfortable experience when appropriate.

There is a strange irony to this stage of my career. I spent years working toward the title of “doctor,” only to immediately become a student again. And I love it. The difference is that now I get to choose what I want to learn and why I want to learn it. Instead of studying because an examination is approaching, I am studying because a patient is sitting in my chair and I want to provide better care. That is a completely different kind of motivation.

More Than Just Wings

The clinical learning curve is only half of the equation. Dental school taught me how to diagnose disease, develop treatment plans, perform procedures, and manage patients. What it didn’t fully prepare me for was the intricate system that surrounds the dentistry itself.

One of the most eye-opening differences has been treatment acceptance. In dental school, it was easy to explain the value of an extraction when the patient’s cost was $39. The clinical conversation was similar, but the financial conversation was entirely different. Now, when I recommend comprehensive treatment, I may be asking a patient to make a financial commitment of thousands of dollars. I’ve had to learn how to communicate the value of treatment honestly and confidently while giving patients the information they need to make decisions that are right for them.

I’m also learning that there is an entire ecosystem operating around every appointment. Scheduling, financial arrangements, insurance, documentation, laboratory communication, inventory, sterilization, ordering, and team coordination all have to work together for the practice to function well. When everything runs smoothly, much of that work is invisible to the doctor. Now, I’m beginning to appreciate just how much goes into creating that seamless patient experience.

Having an experienced team around me has been incredibly empowering. Their knowledge allows me to focus my attention on the clinical side while I gradually learn the systems that support it. Yet, there is still a voice in the back of my mind telling me I need to know all of it. I quickly remind myself that it will come with time.

Finding My Flight Path

Looking back, I think I misunderstood what it meant to be prepared.

I thought preparation meant eventually reaching a point where I would know enough, feel confident enough, and have enough experience to handle anything that came through the door. Now I understand that point probably doesn’t exist. There will always be a new material, a new technique, a more complex patient, a difficult conversation, or a business problem I have never encountered before.

The goal isn’t to eliminate uncertainty. The goal is to become comfortable navigating it. I still have moments when I need to step out of the operatory and search my memory for an answer. I still have systems to learn and procedures to refine. I still have an enormous list of CE courses I want to take. But there is a fundamental difference now. I am no longer preparing to become a dentist. I am becoming a better one.

The transition from dental student to dentist has been humbling, challenging, and at times overwhelming. But it has also been incredibly rewarding. Every day, I get a little more comfortable making decisions, a little more efficient navigating the practice, and a little more confident in the doctor I am becoming.

The cocoon was dental school. It gave me the foundation, the skills, and the knowledge to take flight.

Now, for the first time, I get to decide where I fly.

Join me as I continue my journey into the world of dentistry, learning, growing, and advancing patient care.
